rationale: A wins because it gives the founder sharper reporter-ready tensions and better kill criteria. Its line “ads at a $1B run rate while grocery-delivery order growth slid to single digits” is the real story; B’s “what is this company actually now” is clean, but more familiar. The caveat: A also accepts “the grocery aisle's newest ad surface,” which is a fact-risk B correctly refuses, so this is not a victory parade.
gaps_in_A: “A cart that watches what you put in it is now the grocery aisle's newest ad surface” outruns the update. The facts say carts track items and ads come from 6,000 brands; they do not say carts carry ads or power ad targeting.
“item-level, in-aisle behavioral data” is loaded. The update supports item tracking, not the advertising-data use case A implies.

“few hundred stores across a 1,500-plus banner network” risks implying the cart deployment spans those banners. The update only says Instacart has 1,500+ retail banners and carts are live in a few hundred stores.
The refused investor angle is too quickly dismissed as a duplicate. A markets-desk revenue-mix story can be distinct from an ad-trade retail-media story.
gaps_in_B: “Why 1,500 grocery banners are renting their tech stack instead of building it” overclaims. Partnering with Instacart does not prove banners are renting a full stack or rejecting in-house builds.
“slowing core, accelerating adjacency” invents acceleration. The update gives slowed order growth and a $1B ad run rate, not ad growth velocity.
“The checkout line is quietly disappearing from a few hundred grocery stores” is a tidy headline, but too broad. Smart carts skipping checkout does not mean checkout lines are disappearing storewide.
The second angle, “A grocery marketplace built a $1B ad business out of 6,000 brands,” is real but thin unless it gets buyer-side proof. Otherwise it is a milestone brief wearing a trend jacket.
